meta.note: Generic early muzzle-loading smoothbore cannon, representative of 16th-18th century siege and field artillery.
Generic late-WW2-era tank gun, ballistically closest to the German 8.8cm KwK 36 (Tiger I) — used as this dataset's reference point for scaling all other tank/artillery damage values.
World's first purpose-built tank gun; short barrel traded velocity for sponson clearance, so it relied on HE/case shot vs trenches and MGs rather than armor penetration.

meta.platform: Renault FT (first tank with a fully rotating turret)
meta.note: Low-velocity infantry-support gun rather than an anti-armor weapon - WW1 tanks rarely fought other tanks.
Feared for its long effective range and accuracy, but its shorter L/56 barrel gave it less penetration at range than the Panther's smaller-caliber L/70 gun - caliber alone did not decide the matchup.

The long L/70 barrel (70 calibres vs the Tiger's 56) gave the smaller 75mm round a flatter trajectory and higher penetration than the Tiger's 88mm at typical combat ranges - the historical basis for this dataset's caliber-independent damage scaling.
The Wehrmacht's mainstay medium tank gun for most of the war - a moderate-length 75mm that upgunned the Panzer IV enough to threaten Allied mediums.

meta.platform: StuG III Ausf. G (assault gun / tank destroyer)
meta.note: Ballistically identical to the late Panzer IV's gun; the StuG's low, turretless casemate made it an effective ambush tank-killer, reflected here as slightly higher accuracy than the PZ4 despite equal firepower.
One of the most capable tank guns of 1940 - could defeat most contemporary German armor at normal battle ranges, undone more by French doctrine and radios than by the gun itself.
Italy's best wartime tank gun, but the P40 arrived too late and in too few numbers (produced from 1943) to affect the war; earlier Italian mediums like the M13/40 carried a much weaker 47mm gun.

Bonus addition (extra nation) - the gun that shocked the Wehrmacht in 1941; sloped armor and this reliable gun made the T-34 a generational leap even though its raw penetration lagged behind later German guns.

Testing showed the D-10T could defeat a Panther's glacis at 1500m - a clear postwar leap in penetration over WW2-era guns, driven mainly by better ammunition and a longer barrel rather than a dramatically larger bore.

meta.realGun: M68 105mm L/52 (licensed derivative of the British L7)
meta.note: Adopted after testing against a captured Hungarian T-54A showed existing NATO 90mm guns were becoming inadequate; became the standard NATO tank gun for a generation.

The original L7 that the American M68 and German-built Leopard 1 gun were derived from; remained NATO's standard tank gun into the 1980s even after being superseded by 120mm smoothbores on newest designs.
Same L7 gun family as the Centurion and M60; the Leopard 1 favored mobility and a fast, modern fire-control system over armor thickness, reflected here as the best accuracy of the L7-family entries.

The West's first look at a Soviet smoothbore 125mm - superior raw penetration to any NATO 105mm of the era via a very high-velocity fin-stabilized round, but paired with a simpler autoloader and fire-control system than Western designs, hence the lower accuracy here despite the bigger punch.

meta.realGun: Licensed/reverse-engineered copy of the Soviet D-10T, 100mm L/53.5
meta.note: Ballistically near-identical to the Soviet T-54 it was copied from, but China kept upgrading the Type 59's fire control and ammunition domestically for decades after the Sino-Soviet split, when it could no longer rely on Soviet support.

meta.realGun: 125mm smoothbore gun + autoloader, locally retrofitted in place of the original 100mm D-10T
meta.note: A real, documented Iraqi field modification: rather than replace their huge T-55/Type 59 fleet outright, Iraqi arsenals rearmed some hulls with the same 125mm gun and autoloader family used on the T-72, giving an older, lighter tank a much heavier punch — at the cost of the fire-control sophistication a purpose-built 125mm tank would have, reflected here in lower accuracy than the dedicated T72_EARLY_125MM entry.

meta.realAmmoNote: 3BM9 APFSDS — a Soviet round withdrawn from Soviet service in 1973
meta.note: Same tank and gun as the standard early T-72, but Iraq's actual wartime stocks reportedly relied on older 3BM9 APFSDS ammunition that the Soviets themselves had already retired by 1973 — a real, documented ammunition-supply gap (driven by embargoes and export restrictions) rather than any difference in the gun or vehicle itself, hence the lower damage versus T72_EARLY_125MM despite sharing the same platform.

Real weapon: uniquely among modern Western MBTs, Britain kept a RIFLED 120mm gun (everyone else uses smoothbore) because it fires a heavier HESH round in addition to APFSDS — a genuine doctrinal fork, not an upgrade path other nations skipped by mistake.
Real weapon: the Leclerc was the first Western tank fielded with a bustle autoloader, cutting crew to 3 and enabling one of the fastest sustained rates of fire of any modern MBT.

Real weapon: the A6 upgrade lengthened the standard Leopard 2 gun from L/44 to L/55 — a longer barrel that increases muzzle velocity (and therefore penetration) without changing the caliber at all, the exact same physics principle behind the Panther/Tiger comparison earlier in this dataset.

Real weapon: the M256 is a licensed derivative of the original Rheinmetall gun that also equipped the early Leopard 2 — the two tanks share the same gun family despite representing rival NATO tank programs.

Real weapon: one of the newest MBT designs in this dataset, with an autoloader and an in-arm suspension that lets the tank 'kneel' to change its firing angle — reflected here as the highest accuracy among the modern tank guns.

Real weapon: uniquely places the engine at the front of the hull rather than the rear, specifically to add an extra layer of protection for the crew — a design choice driven directly by Israel's combat experience valuing crew survivability.

meta.realGun: M68 105mm rifled gun (the same gun fitted to Egypt's own M60A3 fleet), replacing the original Soviet 100mm D-10T
meta.note: Real, documented program (started 1984 with US firm Teledyne Continental, ~260-425 hulls converted): the mirror image of the Iraqi QM2 upgrade in this dataset — Iraq bolted a Soviet 125mm gun onto an old T-55, Egypt bolted an American 105mm gun onto the same base tank, each choosing whichever gun matched the rest of their existing fleet's logistics.

Real weapon: M4 Sherman's 75mm M3 gun — reliable and produced in huge numbers, but famously under-gunned against late-war German heavy tanks like the Tiger and Panther already in this dataset, a gap Allied crews partly closed through sheer numerical superiority.

Real weapon: the up-gunned T-34/85, fitted with an 85mm ZiS-S-53 gun from 1944 onward after the original T-34/76 (already in this dataset) proved unable to reliably defeat the frontal armor of German Tigers and Panthers.

Real weapon: the British Churchill infantry tank — slow but very heavily armored by 1940s standards, later marks re-armed with a 75mm gun to give it a fighting chance against German armor it was otherwise built to survive rather than defeat.

Real weapon: the Chieftain was the first NATO tank armed with a 120mm gun (the rifled L11A5) — the direct ancestor of the rifled gun tradition Britain continued into the Challenger 2 already in this dataset.

Real weapon: IS-3, a Soviet heavy tank with a distinctive low 'pike nose' turret; its 1945 Berlin victory parade appearance alarmed Western observers and helped drive early Cold War tank development. Its 122mm gun used slow, separately-loaded ammunition, limiting rate of fire despite its raw punch.
Real weapon: T-90, Russia's main modern MBT — an evolution of the T-72 lineage (already in this dataset) with a more modern 2A46M gun, improved fire control, and explosive reactive armor.

Real weapon: Type 99, China's most advanced domestically-developed MBT, mounting a 125mm smoothbore gun with autoloader — completing this dataset's arc from the Type 59 (a Soviet T-54 copy) through decades of independent Chinese tank development.
